There is no use talking about a deficit that has to be recouped by a tax like this when the government is still piling up surpluses.
The Postmaster General makes the argument that the people who use the mails should be the ones who pay for it. If he is going to use that argument I would, draw particular attention to the use that is made of the postal service by newspapers and periodicals, for which they do not pay the full cost. I will not go further than that. One of my colleagues will have some interesting and very pertinent statistics to lay before the house on that point.
But at any rate the minister says that if the post office is financed in such a way that there is a deficit, that has to be made up out of general revenue, and that that would be a case of making the people who did not use the mails pay for those who did. May I suggest that there is a very close relationship between the incomes of people and the question of whether they use the mails. When you talk about people who do not write very many letters, they are the people whose incomes are low. They are not paying directly into the general funds of the country because they have not sufficient income to put them in the income tax bracket. If deficits are incurred by the post office which have to be met out of the general revenue, I suggest that the burden of those deficits will fall on those who are in the income tax

Post Office Act
brackets, both individuals and corporations, and that that is a fairer way in which to deal with the financing of a service of this kind.
Earlier this afternoon the Postmaster General said that nobody had tried to meet that argument. I think I have met it. I think that this matter should be looked upon not as a commercial operation that has to stand on its own feet but rather as a service to the nation to be treated as one of many services, with the financing of it to be looked at in the light of the whole picture.
The Postmaster General tells us that the increased postage rate will result in this increased revenue of $14 million. In arriving at that estimate I wonder whether he has taken into account the fact that there will be some falling oil in the use of the mails. As the cost of any product goes up, there is a tendency for less of that product to be purchased.
Another question I raise is this. The Postmaster General says that there will be $14 million increased revenue to the Post Office Department by virtue of these increases in postal rates. I do not know what percentage of the postal business is done by business firms as compared with that done by private individuals but I imagine that business mail constitutes the lion's share of the mail of this country. But even if only half of the mail is business mail, that means that $7 million out of this $14 million which is anticipated will be paid by business firms. Most business firms are already paying corporation income tax. Therefore you have to assume that there will be these further exemptions claimed, perhaps for that additional $7 million, and if the rate of taxation is 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 50 per cent, you are going to lose another $2 million, $3 million or $31 million in income tax by virtue of this extra charge that is made by the imposition of this increased rate. Hence the gain to the Post Office Department will be a loss to the Department of National Revenue in the collection of income tax and we shall have some more juggling which may well result, of course, when another election comes around, in a reduction of the postage rate once again.
There is one other comment I wish to make with regard to this increase, and it arises out of the fact that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace this afternoon referred to the fact that in 1942 the postage rate on first-class letters going from one city to another was only 3 cents. He pointed out that the rate was raised in that year from 3 cents to 4 cents, and now it is being raised again from 4 cents to 5 cents. There is in that

procedure a bit of a trick which hon. members should recognize. When the rate was raised from 3 cents to 4 cents in 1942 in the case of letters going from one area to another or from 2 cents to 3 cents in the case of letters within the same area, that raise was made not by the Postmaster General of that day and not by the Post Office Department. It was made by Mr. Ilsley. The then Minister of Finance put that extra cent on as a tax to raise money for purposes of the war. I well remember how Mr. Ilsley made it clear time and time again that the charge for mailing letters, in so far as post office revenue was concerned, had not been increased but that a war tax of one cent had been put on the 2 cent rate making it 3 cents, and on the 3 cent rate making it 4 cents.
The fact that that one cent was a tax obtained right down until 1951. It is only two and a half years ago, when the Post Office Act was being amended, that that increased amount-that tax-was built into the actual postage rate. Down until 1951 the official postage rate was still 2 cents and 3 cents, with one cent tax; but in 1951 the 2 cents was raised to 3 cents and the 3 cents was raised to 4 cents. Now, only two and a half years later, we are getting this further raise to 4 cents and 5 cents. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that all of the statements that have been made about the percentage of increase involved in these higher wages are well put. In fact, I believe that the story is even worse than members have suggested thus far and that this is a resolution which this committee should turn down.

I think on the whole the Canadian people have reason to be proud of the outstanding service performed by the Post Office Department for many years. I have had very happy associations with the postal personnel in my constituency and the post office officials in Ottawa. Nevertheless I think this is a very unfortunate piece of legislation to bring before parliament. I have two opinions to express for what they are worth and I present them in the hope that the Post Office Department will be relieved of the blame that unfortunately will be attached to it for this very unpopular increase in postage rates.
While I was in Ottawa from 1940 to 1949 I made some study of the very large number

Post Office Act
of post offices in Canada where there was very little revenue. In the 1952 report of the Postmaster General I notice that there are 160 post offices in my own province of Saskatchewan where total sales of postage stamps for the previous year were less than $100-$11.50, $13, $12.64, $16.06, $9.20, and so on. I think it would be difficult to argue that, where postage sales are less than $1 a month, there is very good reason in this day and age for continuing considerable public expenditures in maintaining offices in these communities. I realize that patronage enters into the picture, that supporters of the government are given post offices, and that it probably is not easy to change the practice. But before asking all the taxpayers of Canada to accept such a heavy burden as is involved in a 25 per cent increase on the four-cent rate and a 33 J per cent increase on the three-cent rate we should have a look at the very large number of post offices in Canada that might have been justified fifty years ago but certainly are not justified today when so many people have cars and when there are obviously so few people making use of these services.
The second point I want to mention is found in the report that the Postmaster General presented in 1952. There are two pies offered in this report. I am sorry that they do not appear in the 1953 report. One pie is receipts, the other disbursements. In the first case newspapers and periodicals pay for a five cent piece of pie. They give a five cent pie to the Post Office Department but when they want to eat their pie they want an 18J cent piece. I submit to hon. members that it might have been argued fifty years ago that newspapers should be subsidized by the Post Office Department, but in this day and age when daily newspapers have fallen into the hands of a few very wealthy corporations that control not only chains of newspapers but radio stations, I think there is no justification for asking the Post Office Department to take a five cent pie from newspapers and periodicals and dish out an 18J cent pie. On the basis of the year's revenue there is a loss of over $16 million in connection with this one item.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned, in view of the fact that so many of these papers and periodicals carry such a heavy volume of advertising I think we cannot justify subsidizing to this extent. I for one take strong objection to the very large amount of liquor advertising now appearing in so many Canadian periodicals. I object to having such periodicals come to my home at public expense inasmuch as the Post Office
rMr. Nicholson.]
Department is subsidizing them to the tune of $16 million per year. I do not have these figures from the minister, but on the basis of the picture of the pie appearing in his report, taking the amount of receipt for that year as $122 million-I am sure he will correct me if I am wrong-it is my conclusion that the loss in connection with these two items for the year reviewed in his report is $16 million.
In the same pie we notice ordinary letters, and this affects the people who are taking the rap in this latest increase. The figure is 46 cents and it only costs 29 cents to buy their piece of pie. The vast majority of those people in their small homes do not use the air mail facilities to any great extent. They remember that it is only a few months ago that the government came out, shortly before the election, as the great benefactor of the people. At that time they took the excise tax off cheques. They were posing as a tax-reducing government, one that the people should support.

Post Office Act
Then, they do not like it for the further reason that they know second-class mail is being subsidized while the little fellow who writes the first-class mail is having to pay the shot. The increased costs which this government is encountering all along the line did not develop overnight. For years the party to which 1 belong has raised its objections in the House of Commons to the removal of price controls, thus permitting the cost of doing business and the cost of living to continue skyrocketing.
We tried to warn the government that if it did that there would have to be increased costs along with it, and that many of those costs would become permanent. Now we see the cost of living going up, the cost of doing business going up and wages will have to go up. In the light of these facts the government has to come back to tax the people.
The same is true of the increased cost of production of those commodities which our people have to sell. Those production costs have gone so high because the government would not hold the line. When price controls were in force, and when costs could have been kept down, the government did not permit that condition to continue. At this time, with possible recession facing us, and with constant difficulties in selling our products, the government is continuing with these increases. This is just one further evidence of that process.
It is the same story all along the line. The attempt now is to make this increase a permanent one. The Canadian people are now asked to pay for what the government failed to do when it should have been watching costs and keeping them in line.

Mr. Chairman, reference has been made to the increase in wages for postal employees. I cannot think of any group of employees in this country to whom wage increases were so long overdue. I think it rather shameful that the government should seek to use this rather modest wage increase, and the undertaking to have the 40-hour week in certain localities, as an excuse throughout the country for this increase in postal rates.
Some reference has been made to the postal service. If there has been any inefficiency, it is not too difficult to understand when we consider the poor working conditions and the very low wages which have been paid to the postal workers over the past few years. I believe we will have increased efficiency when those workers receive better wages and when there are better working conditions.
[Mr. Castleden.l
One important principle is involved here, just as important as the increase itself. Two ministers of the government have stated that the people of Canada expect the post office to pay for itself. There are two ways of looking at the Post Office Department. Either it will be considered as a public service to provide a very valuable service for the people in this far-flung country or it is going to be considered simply as a commercial venture.
If the government takes the stand that the Post Office Department must pay for itself, then I must ask, in all sincerity, how it can reconcile, on the one hand, the fact that it subsidizes second-class mail, with the argument, on the other, that the post office must pay its own way. You cannot have it both ways. If you believe the post office should be operated strictly along business lines, then logically you must expect the publishers of newspapers and periodicals throughout the country to pay the cost of transmitting their materials through the mails.
I am not going to debate the question as to whether that is advisable or not. What I am saying is that if you accept the principle of subsidizing second-class mail, then you cannot in the next breath offer the argument that the post office ought to pay its own way. You cannot have it both ways. Either the post office is going to pay its way, in which case second-class mail must bear its fair share of the cost of transportation throughout the country, or it will not pay its way.
I suggest that before we have a vote we should have an explanation from the government as to what its attitude is. We must have a clear understanding. If the post office is to be regarded as a commercial venture, one which is to be self-supporting, then I must ask the minister in all sincerity how he justifies a subsidy on second-class mail.

I should like to add only a few words in this discussion. Throughout the country we have had in the past decade a great deal of commercial prosperity. I should like to get in the last extra word here. This discussion today, Mr. Chairman, has been very much like the unfolding of a mystery story along the lines of those written by Erie Stanley Gardner and Mickey Spillane. I have been very interested in listening to the debates today and to get into that mystery of the Canadian post office. As a matter of fact, to use the analogy of a mystery story, what we have unfolded here today has been the story of the hidden subsidy of the post office, and who subsidizes whom, how and why.
Post Office Act
In that regard, Mr. Chairman, it came as a surprise to me, and I am sure it will to the people of Canada, that in the first of our many subsidies connected with the Canadian post office we have those who for many years past have been attaching a three-cent excise stamp or postage stamp to every cheque that they issued. As a result that subsidy has been paid by those who write cheques in order to help subsidize the post office operation, to the tune, I understand from the minister, of some $7,500,000 a year.
The next subsidy that became apparent today in the discussion seems to be the subsidy which has been paid and continues to be paid by the Post Office Department to help support that other arm of government, the Trans-Canada Air Lines. One hon. member brought out some figures which indicated that from the post office revenues the Trans-Canada Air Lines are receiving $5 million or more a year. The T.C.A. is being paid that amount by the post office to carry mail at a rate some four times the rate charged by the same Trans-Canada Air Lines for the transporting of normal air cargo.
Then there appears to be a third type of subsidy, namely, the subsidy that is being paid by the post office to help along other government departments, the franking privilege. That amounts to somewhere around $4 million or $5 million a year, which should properly be charged to all departments of government rather than against the users of the postal service of this country.
We then come to a fourth subsidy, namely, the subsidy paid by the post office to help provide Canadians with their newspapers and periodicals, the second-class mail. It was mentioned today that in the handling of second-class mail the post office shows a deficit of some $28 million a year.
Then we have another subsidy, namely the subsidy paid by the post office to subsidize third-class mail, circulars and the like. Perhaps we should include in the third-class mail such things as Christmas cards. I understand that they come in that category, provided they are unsealed. Since that type of business comes at a particular time of the year, I think it might rank as one of the small things that government might very well do for the people who make government possible. Then we come to another subsidy again. It has been disclosed here as the subsidy which the taxpayers through the Department of Public Works are passing on to the Post Office Department by the provision of postal buildings to the Post Office Department across the country.

Post Office Act
We now come, sir, to the increase in postal rates, and here we have another new type of subsidy, or rather an extension of former types of subsidy. Those who load the mail with love letters and the like are now going to be asked to increase the subsidies they will pay to help keep this post office on an *even keel. Well, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that we have a conglomeration of subsidies: the Post Office Department subsidizes Trans-Canada Air Lines, and other departments of government with the franking privilege, and the Department of Public Works subsidizes the Post Office Department in the provision of buildings; the newspapers and periodicals are being subsidized through rates which certainly do not meet the cost of providing this service; and now we have this new proposal for increased postal rates which are presumably going to yield something like $14 million in extra revenue in order to permit the Post Office Department to break even. Now that we have eliminated one subsidizer, the writer of cheques, who no longer has to put that three-cent stamp on a cheque, we find that the Post Office Department has lost $7,500,000 in the past year. But, Mr. Chairman, in the attempt to break down the new revenue of $14 million which it is expected will come from this proposed increase in postal rates, I have been wondering who is actually going to pay this cost, so I should like to take one specific case of a business of which I have some personal knowledge. This business is located in the west and uses the first-class mail a great deal. Its cost of postage is going to increase slightly over $3,000 a year, but that company is not going to lose $3,000 a year. As it turns out, it can take a tax write-off on the extra postage it is going to be charged of $1,500 through reduced corporation taxes. Then the shareholders of the company with their present taxable position will find that on their personal taxes on the dividends accruing they will save another $600. In other words, in the case of this particular company, while there will be an increase in the payment to the Post Office Department of $3,000, approximately $2,100 will come out of the hands of the federal government through reduced tax income.
The result is that the company will actually pay only about $900 or 30 per cent of the total increased postal charges while the federal government will be providing the other 70 per cent. In the case of individuals who write the occasional letter they will find their postal costs increased 25 or 40 per cent, but that will not amount to very much money.
Is the Post Office Department in a position to give us an estimate as to what proportion
[Mr. Niekle.l
of this $14 million added revenue is going to be offset by reduced tax income to the federal government, in effect being paid by other government departments? In other words, to what extent is this $14 million which is to go to the Post Office Department going to be another subsidy paid by other departments of government?
It seems to me that it would be far better if instead of increasing the postal rates at this time the government reviewed carefully all these hidden subsidies that are now reflected in the operations of the Post Office Department. If the handling of second-class mail, newspapers and periodicals at present rates is justified as a form of subsidy, then that subsidy should be included openly in the accounts of this government instead of being paid for by the users of first-class postal service.
Let us look at all these other subsidies. When we have added them all together, the subsidies paid by the post office and the subsidies paid to the post office, let us try to determine whether the Post Office Department cannot be self-sufficient and operate at a profit without the increased postal rates proposed in this measure.
